characters.identity_anchors: Adult male; exact age, height, build, hair, and facial features unspecified in the text. Defining stable traits are psychological and sensory: dreadfully nervous yet insisting he is not mad; disease-sharpened senses, above all acute hearing (hears things in heaven, earth, and hell). Moves with extreme caution and dissimulation; capable of hearty daytime manner and stealthy midnight motion.
characters.source_evidence: True!—nervous—very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad? The disease had sharpened my senses—not destroyed—not dulled them. Above all was the sense of hearing acute. I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad? Hearken! and observe how healthily—how calmly I can tell you the whole story. (P3). I loved the old man. He had never wronged me... For his gold I had no desire. I think it was his eye! (P4). You should have seen how wisely I proceeded—with what caution—with what foresight—with what dissimulation I went to work! I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I killed him. (P5).
characters.voice_label: intimate tense confessional; controlled and persuasive at first, rising through agitation to foaming raving and final shriek

wardrobe_variants.description: Neat ordinary daytime house clothes of a modest mid-19th-century man; composed enough to speak heartily and unsuspiciously each morning.
source_facts: I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I killed him.
every morning, when the day broke, I went boldly into the chamber, and spoke courageously to him, calling him by name in a hearty tone, and inquiring how he has passed the night.
wardrobe_variants.creative_direction: Simple period shirt, waistcoat, and trousers in muted tones; tidy and unremarkable to support the performance of kindness. Book is silent on exact garments, colors, or fabrics—choose restrained 1840s domestic dress with no blood or disorder.

wardrobe_variants.description: Dark quiet night attire enabling extreme stealth with a closed dark lantern; soft movement, no light-catching detail.
source_facts: every night, about midnight, I turned the latch of his door and opened it—oh, so gently!
I put in a dark lantern, all closed, closed, that no light shone out, and then I thrust in my head.
I moved it slowly—very, very slowly, so that I might not disturb the old man’s sleep.
Upon the eighth night I was more than usually cautious in opening the door.
wardrobe_variants.creative_direction: Matte dark coat or robe over simple clothes; footwear implied soft for silence. Book does not describe night garments—default to period-appropriate dark stealth clothing that reads cunning and careful, never theatrical.

wardrobe_variants.description: Outwardly composed clothes when admitting police (light heart, smile, singular ease); progressive dishevelment as pallor, headache, pacing, foaming, and raving overtake him.
source_facts: I went down to open it with a light heart,—for what had I now to fear?
I smiled,—for what had I to fear?
I was singularly at ease.
I felt myself getting pale and wished them gone. My head ached
I foamed—I raved—I swore! I swung the chair upon which I had been sitting, and grated it upon the boards
There was nothing to wash out—no stain of any kind—no blood-spot whatever. I had been too wary for that. A tub had caught all
wardrobe_variants.creative_direction: Same night or hastily ordered day clothes; initially neat enough to welcome officers and sit in triumph above the corpse. Allow collar, hair, and posture to disorder with mounting terror. No visible bloodstains (book states tub caught all). Book silent on exact post-labor dress.

characters.identity_anchors: Elderly man; the sole specified physical feature is his eye—pale blue with a film over it, the eye of a vulture—which makes the narrator’s blood run cold. No canonical hair, build, height, or other facial detail. Harmless housemate who never wronged or insulted the narrator; possesses treasures/gold the narrator does not desire.
characters.source_evidence: I loved the old man. He had never wronged me. He had never given me insult. For his gold I had no desire. I think it was his eye! yes, it was this! He had the eye of a vulture—a pale blue eye, with a film over it. Whenever it fell upon me, my blood ran cold (P4). for seven long nights... I found the eye always closed... it was not the old man who vexed me, but his Evil Eye (P5). It was open—wide, wide open... all a dull blue, with a hideous veil over it that chilled the very marrow in my bones; but I could see nothing else of the old man’s face or person (P11). Yes, he was stone, stone dead... His eye would trouble me no more (P13).
characters.voice_label: frail elderly; one startled cry “Who’s there?”; one shriek only; low stifled groan of mortal terror; otherwise silent

wardrobe_variants.description: Simple sleeping clothes in bed; covers as he lies asleep or sits up listening in terror; later body dragged to floor and covered by the heavy bed.
source_facts: he lay upon his bed
he moved on the bed suddenly, as if startled
the old man sprang up in bed, crying out—“Who’s there?”
he was still sitting up in the bed listening
I dragged him to the floor, and pulled the heavy bed over him
First of all I dismembered the corpse. I cut off the head and the arms and the legs.
wardrobe_variants.creative_direction: Plain period nightshirt (white or off-white); frail elderly frame. Book silent on exact garment. After death: clinical dismemberment only as stated—no gore spectacle; parts deposited between scantlings, never lingered on. Eye remains the visual anchor while he lives.

characters.identity_anchors: Three adult men acting as a unit; no individual names, ranks, ages, or physical descriptions in the text. Introduced with perfect suavity; manner convinces them the narrator is at ease; they sit, chat of familiar things, smile pleasantly, and remain composed while the narrator breaks down.
characters.source_evidence: there came a knocking at the street door... There entered three men, who introduced themselves, with perfect suavity, as officers of the police. A shriek had been heard by a neighbour during the night; suspicion of foul play had been aroused; information had been lodged at the police office, and they (the officers) had been deputed to search the premises. (P16). The officers were satisfied. My manner had convinced them. I was singularly at ease. They sat, and while I answered cheerily, they chatted of familiar things. (P18). And still the men chatted pleasantly, and smiled. Was it possible they heard not? (P19).
characters.voice_label: calm official suavity; polite introductions and search; thereafter pleasant familiar chat and smiles; no accusation until after the confession

wardrobe_variants.description: Matching or similar mid-19th-century civic/police officer attire marking them as official searchers; neat and authoritative.

Book gives zero uniform detail—default to sober civic authority look. They remain outwardly pleasant and smiling through the narrator’s agony.

And then, when I had made an opening sufficient for my head, I put in a dark lantern... and then I thrust in my head... It took me an hour to place my whole head within the opening (P5); Upon the eighth night I was more than usually cautious in opening the door. A watch’s minute hand moves more quickly than did mine... I kept pushing it on steadily, steadily (P6).

locations.canonical_name: the floorboards / scantlings under the chamber
locations.source_evidence: I then took up three planks from the flooring of the chamber, and deposited all between the scantlings. I then replaced the boards so cleverly, so cunningly, that no human eye—not even his—could have detected any thing wrong. There was nothing to wash out—no stain of any kind—no blood-spot whatever. I had been too wary for that. A tub had caught all—ha! ha! (P15); placed my own seat upon the very spot beneath which reposed the corpse of the victim (P17); tear up the planks!—here, here!—It is the beating of his hideous heart! (P20).

locations.source_evidence: I put in a dark lantern, all closed, closed, that no light shone out (P5); I undid the lantern cautiously—oh, so cautiously—cautiously (for the hinges creaked)—I undid it just so much that a single thin ray fell upon the vulture eye (P5); my thumb slipped upon the tin fastening, and the old man sprang up in bed (P7); I resolved to open a little—a very, very little crevice in the lantern. So I opened it—you cannot imagine how stealthily, stealthily—until, at length a single dim ray, like the thread of the spider, shot from out the crevice and fell full upon the vulture eye (P10); With a loud yell, I threw open the lantern and leaped into the room (P13).
